fields.meta_title: SaaS Landing Page Examples and Build Guide | Emergent
fields.meta_description: Four SaaS landing page examples past the homepage, what makes software buyers sign up, and how Emergent builds each page with its data.
fields.h1: Build a SaaS Landing Page and the App Behind It
fields.hero_description: Tell Emergent what the product does and who buys it. It builds the SaaS landing page, the signup form and a table of every new account.
fields.features_heading: What Ships With Each SaaS Page
fields.features_subheading: The sections a software buyer reads, plus the signup data and follow-up rules your team works from after launch.
fields.feature_1:
Every section from one description

Describe the product and the one action you want from its buyer. Emergent writes every section down to the signup form, and you change any of them by sending another message.
fields.feature_2:
Signups saved to a table you own

Each signup becomes a row in your own database, stamped with the plan picked and the campaign that sent the visit. Filter and export the rows, or sync each new one to your CRM.
fields.feature_3:
Calculators that run your formula

Write the math as a sentence, such as seats times price minus the annual discount. Emergent builds the inputs and the result, then saves each calculation next to the visitor's email.
fields.feature_4:
A second headline on request

Ask for a variant with a different headline or a shorter form. Emergent builds it, splits visitors between the two and records which version each new account saw on its visit.
fields.feature_5:
Alerts for the accounts that matter

Set a rule such as a work email domain or a team of 50 or more. When a signup matches, its owner gets a Slack message or an email with the details as soon as the row is saved.
fields.feature_6:
Code that leaves with you

The page code and the tables behind it export to your GitHub repository. Host on Emergent with a custom domain, which uses credits, or deploy the export beside the app you ship.
fields.why_title: Why Build SaaS Pages With Emergent?
fields.why_description: Landing page builders host the page and keep signups in their dashboard. Emergent builds the page and its signup data as code you own.

fields.usecase_heading: Four SaaS Pages Beyond the Homepage
fields.tab_content_1:
Fifty requests, then the product manager hears about it

Plumline sells invoicing software to contractors, and its integrations page shows a Request button for every tool it does not support. Each request is saved with the tool name and the company asking. When a tool reaches 50 requests, product manager Dana Ruiz gets a Slack direct message naming those companies.
fields.tab_content_2:
The calculator puts $4,500 a month on timesheets

Agency owners on Tidewell's calculator page enter their team size, the hours each person spends on timesheets and their billing rate. A team of 25 at three hours a month and $60 an hour comes to 75 hours, or $4,500. An email field under the result sends the estimate and saves the inputs with the lead.
fields.tab_content_3:
Release notes reach only the readers who asked

Every reader of Quarry's changelog can subscribe and tick the topics they follow, such as Reporting or Integrations. A release tagged Reporting goes only to the 1,240 subscribers who picked Reporting and skips the other 2,660. Each send is logged against the release in the subscriber table.
fields.tab_content_4:
Agencies with 10 clients get a partner manager

Applications to the Stackwise partner program ask how many client accounts an agency manages. An agency with 10 or more goes to partner manager Ken Adeyemi as an email with the application attached. Smaller agencies receive the self-serve partner kit by return email and can reapply as they grow.

fields.howto_title: How to Build a SaaS Landing Page
fields.howto_description: Galleries show how a page looks. These steps cover what it asks of the visitor and what you measure once traffic arrives.
fields.howto_step_1_title: 01 Pick the one action the page asks for
fields.howto_step_2_title: 02 Name the buyer in the headline
fields.howto_step_3_title: 03 Show the product doing that job
fields.howto_step_1_des: Decide whether visitors start a trial, book a demo or join a waitlist, and build the page around that single button. Landing pages usually drop the site navigation for the same reason: every extra link is a way out before the visitor acts.
fields.howto_step_2_des: Write the headline for one buyer and one job. Invoicing for contractors who wait 60 days to get paid tells a roofer more than a line about the future of finance. Put the product category in the subhead so nobody has to guess what you sell.
fields.howto_step_3_des: Use screenshots or a short screen recording of the actual interface, cropped to the screen that does what the headline promises. Abstract illustrations look polished and explain nothing. A buyer wants to see the screen they will spend their working day in.
fields.howto_step_4_des: Show the plans on the page or link to them from the header, and state what a trial gives the visitor. If a plan needs a sales conversation, say so plainly and give the visitor a way to book one without leaving the page.
fields.howto_step_5_title: 05 Put proof from peers near the button
fields.howto_step_5_des: A named quote from a company the visitor sees as a peer outweighs a wall of logos. Match the proof to the audience: an agency testimonial on a page for agencies, a contractor's numbers on a page for contractors. Place it where hesitation happens, beside the signup.
fields.howto_step_6_des: Every signup field should change what happens next. Team size can decide whether sales gets involved, and a company name can prefill the workspace. Anything else can wait until the person is inside the product and has a reason to answer.
fields.howto_step_7_des: Add utm_source and utm_campaign to every ad and email link, then store both values with each signup. Judge each campaign by how many of its signups become active or paying accounts a month later, not by the signup count on launch day.

plan.angle: The top 10 is inspiration galleries (saaslandingpage.com, Saaspo, Lapa Ninja, Dribbble, Behance, Figma), a Reddit thread, a YouTube teardown and two builder blogs (KlientBoost, Unbounce). They show screenshots of heroes and stop there. This page defines the term up top for the AI Overview, then walks through four pages a SaaS company actually ships besides the homepage (integrations directory, savings calculator, changelog, partner program), each with the data and the follow-up behind it, and answers the PAA questions plainly, ChatGPT ones included.
tab_stories: Plumline, invoicing software for contractors, lists its integrations on one page with a request button, and when a tool reaches 50 requests product manager Dana Ruiz gets a Slack direct message with the companies asking.

Tidewell, time-tracking software for agencies, runs a calculator page where a visitor enters team size and weekly timesheet hours, sees the monthly cost in dollars, and leaves an email to get the estimate.
Quarry, project software, runs a changelog page where readers subscribe by topic, so a Reporting release emails only the 1,240 subscribers who picked Reporting.

Stackwise, marketing analytics software, takes partner applications from agencies, and any agency managing 10 or more client accounts goes to partner manager Ken Adeyemi while the rest get the self-serve partner kit.

claims_to_source: Software as a service (SaaS) is software delivered over the internet, run and maintained by the vendor, and usually paid for by subscription
A landing page is a standalone page built for one campaign or goal, with a single call to action
ChatGPT is a hosted service used in a browser or app, with paid plans sold as monthly subscriptions
ChatGPT can write HTML for a page and preview it inside the chat
Adding utm_source, utm_medium and utm_campaign parameters to a URL lets analytics tools report which campaign sent a visit
